claims.text: Prior simulations of HfNbTaTiZr generally represented nearly defect-free, oxygen-free bulk crystals.
The proposed framework will separately calculate lattice and electronic thermal transport.
The lattice calculation will incorporate atomic-mass disorder, force-constant disorder, defect scattering, and anharmonic phonon interactions.
Electronic thermal transport will be modeled separately using DFT-derived electronic structures.
Site-to-site variations in atomic mass and force constants enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering from mass and force-constant disorder reduces lattice thermal transport independently of electronic conduction paths.
Incorporating atomic-scale disorder and anharmonic interactions into phonon Boltzmann transport overcomes limitations of Debye-type and perfect-crystal estimates.
Separating lattice and electronic transport enables a more precise determination of lattice thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach will improve lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy by roughly 20–30% relative to earlier perfect-crystal and Debye-model methods.
Predicted lattice thermal conductivity will agree with experimental measurements within a 20–30% error margin.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are expected to be nearly equal.
Between 300 and 1200 K, the electronic contribution is expected to dominate total thermal conductivity.
Experiments below 200 K indicate comparable lattice and electronic contributions.
Existing measurements from 300 to 1200 K were made on specimens containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Earlier analytical approaches conflate lattice and electronic heat transport.
The approach is expected to apply from below 200 K through 1200 K for high-purity, oxygen-controlled HfNbTaTiZr.
Prediction accuracy may decrease for oxygen contents above 1 wt.% or for significant extrinsic defect populations.
Electron–phonon coupling and variations in defect distributions introduce residual uncertainty into the separated transport predictions.
Time-domain thermoreflectance can provide an experimentally determined lattice thermal conductivity for the proposed falsification comparison.
A lattice-conductivity deviation greater than approximately 30%, failure of near-equal contributions below 200 K, or failure of electronic dominance at higher temperatures would falsify the approach.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes a 20–30% improvement in accuracy, whereas the predicted outcome specifies a 20–30% absolute error margin. These are different quantities and do not establish the claimed improvement without an explicit baseline error.
